title: PCR-based assays for sexing Silene latifolia and Silene dioica
author: Hewett, Sánchez Vilas, et al.

steps.title: Grind leaf tissue
steps.instruction: Place one ca. 75 mm² disc of fresh leaf tissue in a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube and grind with a micropestle.

steps.title: Add extraction buffer and vortex
steps.instruction: Add 400 µL Edward's extraction buffer (200 mM Tris, 250 mM, 25 mM EDTA, 0.5 % SDS) to the ground tissue, vortex the tube, and incubate at 55 °C for 10 min.

steps.title: Centrifuge and transfer supernatant
steps.instruction: Centrifuge the lysate at 13 000 rpm for 1 min, then transfer 300 µL of the supernatant to a sterilised Eppendorf tube.

steps.title: Precipitate DNA with isopropanol
steps.instruction: Mix the transferred supernatant with 300 µL 100 % isopropanol, let stand at room temperature for 2 min, then centrifuge at 13 000 rpm for 15 min.

steps.title: Remove supernatant and ethanol wash
steps.instruction: Discard the supernatant, add 300 µL 70 % ethanol to the pellet, leave for 3 min, and centrifuge at 13 000 rpm for 5 min.

steps.title: Air‑dry pellet
steps.instruction: Discard the ethanol supernatant and allow the DNA pellet to air‑dry for a few minutes.

steps.title: Resuspend DNA in TE buffer
steps.instruction: Dissolve the dried pellet in 100 µL TE buffer (10 mM Tris, 0.1 mM EDTA).

steps.title: Final incubation and storage
steps.instruction: Incubate the resuspended DNA at 55 °C for 30 min, then store at –20 °C until required.

description: When applied to known-sex plants, both assays (ss816 and ss441) generally provided the predicted outcomes for sexing: genotypic females displayed only the X-specific band, while genotypic males additionally showed the Y-specific band (Figs. 1A; 2A). When using assay ss816 to sex 98 individuals, including samples from UK and Spanish populations of S. latifolia and UK populations of S. dioica, results matched the phenotypic sex in all but 3 cases (Table 2, and see below), corresponding to an error rate of 3.1%. While it does not affect the ability of accurate molecular sexing, it should be noted that in the Spanish population of S. latifolia the X-specific band only amplified in females, but not in males – still yielding the male-specific band in males, and the X band as an amplification in females (Fig. 1B). In addition, using ss816 we obtained clear test results for 163 S. latifolia individuals, with the test providing non-ambiguous results as either male or female for each tested sample. However, since their phenotypic sex was unknown, this merely demonstrated that the assay gave clear, albeit unverified, results for a relatively large number of individuals. Use of ss441 to sex 55 individuals from the same populations yielded assay results that matched the phenotypic sex without any mismatches, giving an error rate of 0% (Table 2). For this assay, S. dioica did not reveal discernible differences between males and females (Fig. 2C), leading to the inability to sex individuals. An additional 40 S. latifolia individuals with unknown phenotypic sex successfully amplified for ss441. Of these 40, 35 matched the sex predicted by assay ss816, and the remaining 5 were solely amplified by ss441.Fig. 1Sex identification results from assay ss816. A.
